bearings.paper_claim: House-majority ties raise contract-firm revenue in 12 of 13 tests; Senate ties in only 3 of 13. In the 2011 House-flip kernel-weighted difference-in-differences, lobbyists at Republican-aligned firms gained just over $10,000 for the year, and ousted Democratic-aligned firms lost more than $40,000 in annual revenue (stated per lobbyist for one year in the key findings). Outcome: revenue per lobbyist; 1,603 contract firms, 2008 Q1-2016 Q3. The 2015 Senate flip shows no significant effect.
bearings.paper_location: p.2 (key findings); p.7-8 (difference-in-differences, Figures 3-4); p.8 Conclusion
bearings.system_side: SEATS-W keeps House and Senate on separate seat scales (sgs_seats.R:24). The brain records one election, the 2022 House, 17 weeks, 538 Lite: -3.47 pp in the Democratic share of giving per +1 expected Democratic seat (block-bootstrap p 0.0086 at 3-week / 0.0174 at 5-week blocks; Holm 0.034 / 0.070), with the Senate showing nothing. The result is EXPLORATORY.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The House-yes, Senate-null pattern in SEATS-W matches the paper's House-over-Senate pattern, which supports chamber-specific estimates. The paper does not predict SEATS-W's sign: it measures contract-lobbying revenue after control actually changed, by firm partisanship; SEATS-W measures the partisan share of giving as within-cycle seat forecasts move. It cannot be cited as evidence for access-seeking in SEATS-W. Both are single-episode designs.

bearings.paper_claim: A change in House control moves contract-lobbying revenue between partisan firms: in 2011 lobbyists at Republican-aligned firms gained just over $10,000 for the year and ousted Democratic-aligned firms lost more than $40,000 in annual revenue (firm-level difference-in-differences on revenue per lobbyist). In Figure 2 (90% threshold, time-fixed measure only) Republican and Democratic firms were roughly at parity, with a marginal advantage to Democratic firms in 2008-2010 and to Republican firms in 2011-2016; bipartisan firms consistently earned greater average revenue.
bearings.system_side: The lobbying card carries outside-firm fees (LDA income_total) and in-house expenses (expenses_total) as separate series, never added. The lobbying refit is sector-aggregate with no partisan or control term: dy ~ dg + factor(year), anchor last_year, clustered by study_sector and year.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper's population (federal contract registrants, registrant differs from client) corresponds to the outside-firm fees series, not in-house expenses. The effect is distributional across firm partisanship; the paper does not identify a sector-total change. A common control shock would be absorbed by factor(year) in the fit but cannot be projected forward. Before adding a control-flip term, test whether outside-firm totals step after the 2011, 2015 and 2019 flips.
bearings.verifier_note: Analyst wrote that Democratic firms 'led' in 2008-2010 and Republican firms in 2011-2016; the paper says the two were 'roughly at parity' with a 'marginal advantage' trading back and forth, and Figure 2 uses only the 90% time-fixed measure. Reworded. Code lines confirmed (379 LOBBY_SERIES; 554 'never added here'; models.json lobby entry at 22-26).

bearings.paper_claim: Firm ties to the House majority are worth approximately $5,000 to $6,000 per lobbyist per quarter in the six levels models (firm random effects, year fixed effects, 2008-2016, N = 33,243 firm-quarters, 1,603 firms); first-differences models give $1,800 to $5,000. Senate effects appear only with the time-fixed measure in the levels models and not at all in first differences.
bearings.system_side: The SHIFT spec (brain) regresses RShare = R/(R+D) of candidate giving on Shift = P - RMajNow (expected minus current Republican control), by recipient chamber. The SHIFT preview (2021-25 window) shows no stable partisan shift: chamber-stacked -0.04, p 0.76; House +0.68 is SATURATED (2023 vs 2025 only); Senate -0.16. The cited sgs_panel.R lines build the SHIFT tables (which store the Democratic share D/(D+R) and expected/current Democratic control), not the regression itself.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The outcomes differ: the paper measures who earns lobbying fees, not where giving goes, and the separate Furnas et al. paper on lobbying/PAC overlap reports minimal overlap between lobbying and campaign-spending organizations. A null SHIFT preview is not contradicted by a lobbying-firm revenue premium. If SHIFT is ever extended to lobbying, key it to realized House control with chambers stratified.

Added the 2021-25 preview window and the House +0.68 value the analyst omitted.

related.why: Bacik reports that registrants employing lobbyists with connections to both parties generate higher income per lobbyist (Fig. S46C) while legislators polarize; this paper finds bipartisan lobbying firms earn the highest average revenue.

Same first author; reports minimal overlap between organizations that lobby and those that make campaign expenditures, which explains why a lobbying-revenue premium need not appear in PAC giving-share tests.
Both build on Lobbying Disclosure Act filings; this paper uses the registrant-versus-client split to isolate contract firms.
Both infer the partisanship or ideology of actors from campaign contribution records.
Kim links campaign donations and lobbying sequentially; this paper uses lobbyists' donations as a partisan identity signal for firms.
The review discusses Bertrand et al. (2014) on connections versus expertise, which this paper extends from individual lobbyists to firms.

summary_issues: Summary: '42% to 60% of firms are partisan' and 'bipartisan firms earn the highest average revenue' omit their bases; the 42-60% range depends on the 85/90/95% cutoffs, and the bipartisan revenue lead comes from Figure 2 at the 90% time-fixed measure only.
Summary: 'Senate alignment matters only under the time-fixed measure' holds for the levels models only; the first-differences models show no Senate support at all.
Summary: the +$10k / -$40k difference-in-differences figures lack their denominator; the paper states them as revenue per lobbyist for one year (2010 to 2011), firm-level.
